paras: The lynching of Macum Marshall was the killing of a Black man by a posse of armed men near Blackshear, Georgia, on November 2, 1888. Marshall was accused of raping Mrs. Henry Howard, a farmer's wife, in her home that morning, and was captured in a nearby swamp and lynched the same day. The story reached readers in Savannah, Kentucky and California as a short wire item.

According to a Blackshear dispatch printed in the Savannah Morning News, Marshall entered the Howard house at 7 o'clock on the morning of November 2 while Henry Howard, described as "a respectable farmer," was away. The dispatch stated as fact that he "forced her to submit to his demand" and then fled to a swamp about a mile from the house. He stayed there until a posse of armed men captured him and, in the paper's words, "avenged the wronged woman by lynching the criminal."
None of the reports names the members of the posse, gives their number, or says how Marshall was killed.
No report of an arrest, an inquest or any official inquiry into the killing appears in the coverage, and no account from Mrs. Howard or her husband was found.

The Savannah Morning News ran the fullest account on November 3 under the headline "Outrage and Lynching" and the deck "The Wife of a Farmer the Victim of a Black Brute." Its report treated the accusation as proven, calling Marshall "the criminal" and presenting the lynching as vengeance on the woman's behalf. A shorter Savannah dispatch, also dated November 2, reduced the story to a single sentence saying Marshall "outraged" Mrs. Howard and "was subsequently lynched."

Kentucky weeklies printed that sentence under the headline "Promptly Lynched," the Big Sandy News on November 8 and the Hickman Courier twice in its November 9 issue. Further afield, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union gave it one line among its "Telegraphic Brevities" on November 5, without names, saying only that a Black man at Blackshear had been lynched "for assaulting a white woman." That brief was the only report to state the woman's race.

reader.title: Lynching of Macum Marshall
bases: A1 reports that a posse of armed men captured Macum Marshall in a swamp and lynched him on an accusation of rape; A2 and A3 also call it a lynching.

A1 says a 'posse of armed men' captured Marshall and 'avenged the wronged woman by lynching the criminal', and A2 and A3 say he was lynched, so an extralegal killing on a rape accusation is reported; the posse's size is not given, but the plural 'armed men' and the word 'lynching' point to a group killing.
All reports trace to Nov. 2 dispatches from Blackshear and Savannah (A1, A3), with A2 a later digest and A4-A5 reprints; no separate local, inquest or follow-up report was found.

Kentucky weeklies ran the Savannah dispatch under 'Promptly Lynched', and the Sacramento Record-Union gave it one line in a column of brevities.

record_check.dossier: 1888-11-02: both dispatches are dated Nov. 2 and place the alleged assault 'this morning', with the lynching following; Nov. 5 is the date of the Sacramento digest.
No county is named in the coverage; only Blackshear is given.
Near Blackshear: the Howard house was 'near Blackshear' and the capture was in a swamp about a mile from the house.

record_check.dossier: Accused of raping Mrs. Henry Howard, a farmer's wife, in her home; only A2 states that she was white.
Fled to a swamp and was captured by the posse, which lynched him; he was never reported in official custody.
Supported: the phrase is the Savannah Morning News's own wording, not a quoted statement by the posse.

Macum Marshall, described as a 'negro man' and 'colored'.
